speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise today, on the eve of International Women's Day, and join with Canadians to mark the gains that women have made toward achieving equality both here in Canada and around the world.
International Women's Day encourages us to reflect on the position of women in our society today and to consider their aspirations for the future. Women in Canada have much to celebrate. We have made great strides in achieving equality in all spheres of society. It has become increasingly clear, indeed, that women's issues are becoming society's issues.
But these gains have not come easily. They are the result of hard work and co-operation. They are the result of women forming effective partnerships to promote ideas and initiate action.
Tomorrow, on International Women's Day, we will honour the spirit of co-operation through this year's theme: "Together Towards Equality".
Partnerships play a critical role in advancing women's equality. Business, labour and government must work closely with women's groups and organizations to make Canada a more understanding and tolerant society. Women must continue to work together, women from all walks of life, including those in the labour force, those working at home, women of colour, elderly women, disabled women, and immigrant women.
As Canada's Minister responsible for the Status of Women, I am proud to co-ordinate our government's initiatives on behalf of Canadian women.

March 7, 1991
Routine Proceedings
Canada also has a proud tradition of actively supporting and promoting equality for women in major international forums. Within the United Nations, we have worked steadfastly to advance the role of women through our long-standing membership on the Commission of the Status of Women currently in session in Vienna. At this session, Canada has pressed for concerted action to address the priority issues of violence against women, education, the environment, and population.
Last October, I had the honour of chairing the meeting of Commonwealth Women's Affairs Ministers here in Ottawa. This meeting provided our Commonwealth friends with an opportunity to exchange views and share in a vision of a world in which gender equality is the norm and not the exception.
Here in Canada, I have met with more than 130 women's groups and many more women individually over the past year to learn first-hand about the issues that concern them. A meeting with representatives of women's centres last year confirmed my belief of the vital role that these centres play in Canadian women's lives.
I was delighted to join with the Secretary of State in January in announcing the continuation of funding for these centres on an ongoing basis.

Mr. Speaker, much progress has been made since the early years of this century, but although barriers to full participation by women in society have been eliminated, discriminatory attitudes, values and behaviour still exist. However, when the Canadian government started its first term, it made a commitment to gradually eliminate these societal problems and has acted accordingly.

Collaborative action among government and non-government sectors has resulted in many substantial gains for women in the past 12 months.
Among these key achievements are the increased parental benefits under the unemployment insurance program. The decision by the Supreme Court of Canada that recognized the battered wife syndrome is a justifiable defence. The initiative taken by the Canadian
Judicial Centre to establish an education program for judges on the subject of gender equality, and the announcement of the closure of the Kingston Prison for Women and its replacement with five regional facilities, including a healing lodge for aboriginal women.
Most significantly the government's renewed family violence initiative provided $136 million to the prevention, education and support for projects to counter violence against women and children, representing more than twice the level of funding committed since 1986.
As well, a parliamentary subcommittee is currently examining these issues as they relate to violence against women and the government's role in dealing with this problem.
Canadian women have much to celebrate, but we also must recognize the challenges they have had. Violence against women must continue to be a major priority. Women must be actively involved in decisions regarding the future shape of Canada and national unity. Women must play an important role in international affairs, bringing their perspective to achieve lasting peace and ensuring women's equality around the world.
Our government is fully committed to promoting the rights of women in Canada. We are committed to creating conditions that will enable women to achieve full and equal participation in our society. We are committed to being active members in a strong, dynamic and productive partnership with women to achieve these goals.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the minister for her comments. I am aware of her interest and her commitment. Indeed it has been shown in the time that she has held this portfolio. But I fear that the actions of this government do not reflect a similar commitment on the part of cabinet, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Finance.
While I do not deny that we have made strides, particularly over the last 20 years, I am afraid it is somewhat like saying: "Well, at least we are still not wearing slave collars".
The unfortunate truth is that in the six and a half years since this government has taken office, the economic status of women has not improved. Indeed, over six and a half years the economic picture has at best remained static and, if it has remained static in the face of increases in the cost of living and in other matters, then
March 7, 1991

we know that the lot of women is worse than it was in 1984.
Women, if we count in professional women-and this is a small percentage-still make 64 cents for every dollar that men make. If we remove professional women from this equation, women make 50 cents for every dollar men make, and this is the vast majority of working women. These statistics have basically remained unchanged since the 1940s.
We know that women are still locked into low paying, pink collar ghetto jobs. They still face systemic discrimination, sexual harassment, glass ceilings, and an over-all attitude that tends to trivialize the work that women do, even when it is paid. When it is unpaid as in the home and in the volunteer sector, it is virtually ignored.
Women work in conditions that most men would not put up with. Like it or not, immigrant women in this country are still left to the mercy of exploiting employers and virtual slave wages. They are locked into a situation that they cannot escape because of a lack of access to English and French as second language training.
It is a sad fact but the ambitions of the average 18-year old man with a high school education can and will be realized, whereas the ambitions of a 20-year old woman with a university degree will put her into a lower salary scale than that young man with only a high school education.
We sit in a country today where one million children go without pre-school and after school care. Latchkey children are one of the disgraces of our society. Six years ago Judge Rosalie Abella in her royal commission report on employment equity said that child care was the bridge to employment equity.
That is no less true, indeed it is more true today than it was six years ago. Still we wait and the women and children of Canada wait for a meaningful national child care program that will bring us accessibility and quality child care across this country.
Over all hangs the spectre of violence against women, of injury and of death. In my own province of Nova Scotia, a small little province where we think of our-
Routine Proceedings
selves as fairly civilized as opposed to the rest of the people in the flesh-pots of central Canada-
That is sexist.

I am not being sexist; I am being geogra-phicalist.
To return to a much more serious point, in Nova Scotia where we tend to think of ourselves as more civilized, we have been proven wrong in this past year because six women have been brutally murdered in the Province of Nova Scotia in the past year. Just last week, the body of a 17-year old girl was found in a garbage dumpster, brutally murdered, in my own metropolitan area of Halifax-Dartmouth. And the statistics go on and on.

Daily life is very difficult for some women in this country. They get no help from the government. They deserve a lot more, and they deserve to get it now.

We need in this country action today. We need a royal commission on violence against women. We need to shine the light in the dark comers to prevent more women and their children being brutalized and killed. We all sat back in horror at the events in Montreal of a year ago last December. But in that same year, 119 women died at the hands of men in this country, and nobody thought to mention those statistics.
In 1970, a royal commission was called on the status of women. It was the catalyst for the women's movement and those very real improvements over the last 20 years, which the minister mentioned in her statement. The time has come to do it again, to look at the problem that is the most crucial, the most urgent, for all of us in our society-the question violence.
I ask this so that those victims in 10 years' time will not have increased and we will not still be crying in the wilderness.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be in the House today and to respond to the minister's statement on the eve of International Women's Day. As the minister said and as the spokesperson for the Liberal Party in the House said, women today do have a number of things to celebrate.

March 7, 1991
Routine Proceedings
We can celebrate the defeat of this government's bill to recriminalize abortion for women in this country; we can celebrate the end of war in the Persian Gulf; and we can celebrate the reinstatement of funding that this government cut to women's centres. These were all defeats, reversals or terminations of government policy.
The Minister responsible for the Status of Women often speaks of partnerships. Her government is creating a partnership between women in this country and poverty. In the middle of a recession it has extended the spending limits on social assistance. It has created a GST, a goods and services tax, an additional tax that no one can afford, least of all single women and lower income women. It has cut spending for health and for education services in our country.
Single mothers and other poor families will find it even more difficult now to feed and clothe their children as a direct result of this government's policies.
The Tories turn their backs on women victims of violence by underfunding programs; by limiting the Canada Assistance Plan, which funds shelters for battered women; by refusing to move on mandatory equality training for judges in a criminal justice system; by allowing violence pornography to continue in our society; by limiting economic options for women; and by cutting affordable housing.
They are adding to the hardships of victims of violence and the hardships of women in our society. They are in fact a part of the problem, not a part of the solution.
By continuing to stall on the enactment of a clause in the Canadian Human Rights Act barring discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, they are further discriminating against a particular sector of women and men in our society.
The Tories are in partnership with employers who in fact exploit immigrant women in our society. They continue to refuse to give immigrant women the same access to language training that is given to male immigrants.
The government has shelved its own gun control legislation. The government is not in partnership with women who are shot and killed with guns that have been
legally obtained, and with ammunition that has been legally obtained. It is not in partnership with the families of these victims of violence.
The Tories are not in partnership with families who have a desperate need for child care and in fact have been promised a child care program in two successive elections, in many speeches by government members on that side of the House. We still have no child care program in Canada.
The government is not in partnership with aboriginal women, aboriginal women who are still tied up in the bureaucracy with Bill C-31.
The Tories are not in partnership with older women living in poverty, unable to have access to their pensions because discrimination still exists in federal pension legislation. In fact, the Conservative government is not in partnership with women at all in this country.
I read the minister's press release. It made me angiy, Mr. Speaker, because she talked about moving together towards equality; equality with women's groups whose funding has been cut; with education, which has also been cut; with all levels of government which are choked by federal cuts in transfer payments; with labour, which it has tried to destroy and continues to try; with concerned citizens to whom it never appears to listen. The minister also talked of many challenges to come, and I have listed many of them in my speech today.
If the government does not have the political will to call for a royal commission on violence against women- we must have a royal commission; the reasons are clear-then step aside and allow Audrey McLaughlin and the New Democratic Party to form a real partnership with the women of this country to work towards economic and social justice in our society.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture) moved
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
that Bill C-98, an act authorizing agreements between the Government of Canada and the provinces to provide for protection for the income of producers of agricultural products and to enable the Government of Canada to take additional measures for

March 7, 1991
Government Orders
that purpose be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to present to the House today Bill C-98 for consideration.
Bill C-98 is an act to provide for enabling legislation to allow provinces and the federal government to engage in the development of programs necessary to support and stabilize agricultural farm income. The short title of the bill is the Farm Income Protection Act.
This enabling legislation will go some distance in providing long-term stability to the agricultural industry. What is significant is that it is the first concrete result in one of the most comprehensive reviews of agricultural policy ever undertaken in this country. It will provide a new system of safety nets for Canadian farmers which will deliver programs and assistance equitably to farmers in all regions of the country. At the same time it will encourage sound farming and business practices, thus ensuring there is a clear response to the market signals of not only the country but, indeed, of the world.
It is important to note in that connection that the principles enshrined in section 4 clearly outline the basis on which agreements with the provinces can be negotiated. It is very important to consider the four principles.
Any agreements which are negotiated must be production or market neutral; second, they must take into account the regional diversity of this country; third, they must be sensitive and compatible to international obligations; and, finally, they must provide and encourage environmental and economic sustainability.
This enabling legislation will provide for the following programs: Gross Revenue Insurance Plan; the Net Income Stabilization Account; the Crop Insurance Program and Revenue Insurance Program; as well as the provision for the establishment of special measures.
This new legislation is built upon the provisions of the existing Crop Insurance Act and that part of the Agricultural Stabilization Act which deals with tripartite price stabilization. With the passage of this bill, the Crop Insurance Act, the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act will be repealed and all
agricultural products will be protected under this one comprehensive act.
Farmers will be able to choose crop insurance, revenue insurance, or both. They will also be able to set aside money in the NISA accounts which the governments will match.
It is important to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the two programs are clearly compatible and complementary with each other. If we are to have long-term stability, confidence and security for the future, it is important that both the GRIP concept-namely, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan-and the Net Income Stabilization Account be implemented together.
I will have a little more to say about that. As it now stands, the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan will provide assistance to producers in the short to medium-term. There is some less degree of urgency in terms of the implementation of the NISA concept. I think if we were to consider the deliberations of the task force that designed these programs they outline the importance of having the two programs working hand in hand.
What is really significant about the legislation that we are introducing today, Mr. Speaker, is the way in which this legislation has been developed. It clearly outlines a first in the development of public policy, and in this case agricultural policy. It is fair to say that this program through the means of this legislation was designed from the ground up by farmers, by provinces and the federal government working together as a result of the policy review process.
This is really the product of the agriculture policy review which was launched in 1989 to take stock of where we are at, to look at our industry, to look into the future and try to implement the kinds of policy and structural changes that may be necessary to provide that kind of security and stability for the 1990s and beyond.
In the course of this we have had the support and the co-operation of many groups, many parties, including the provincial governments. Both federal and provincial governments called for this policy review at the regular meeting of the federal and provincial ministers which was held in Prince Albert in August of 1989. That became the turning point in our attempts to lay a new foundation for a solid, responsive, competitive, diverse
March 7, 1991

and vibrant agricultural industry. It is an important milestone. It is a new approach and it is a comprehensive approach. I hope that as a result of this more comprehensive approach in dealing with the problems of agriculture, we can establish long-term policies and rely to a lesser degree on ad hoc policies.
Colleagues will know that in November 1989 we published the discussion paper Growing Together to set out the course of this review. Literally everyone who had a stake in agriculture became a part of that review process. Growing Together is based upon four pillars: more market responsiveness, greater self-reliance within the agrifood sector, a national policy which recognizes the regional diversity of this country, and increased environmental sustainability.
In December 1989 Agriculture Canada hosted a huge national agrifood policy conference where just under 2,000 delegates from all across the country, reflecting both levels of government and the industry, and all of those involved in the agrifood industry, to come together to talk about a number of issues. We dealt at that time with issues such as food quality and safety, supply management systems, farm finance and management, marketing and trade development, transportation, sustainable agriculture and safety nets.
Following this conference, 11 task forces were established to examine in detail various aspects of agrifood policy. Because of the very serious problems facing the grains and oilseeds sector at that time, it was decided that the committee studying safety nets would be put on the fast track in anticipation of developing a safety net mechanism that would serve the grains and oilseeds but would also be applicable to other commodities.
The federal-provincial industry committee, which I referred to, was formed in January 1990. In May 1990 it presented its preliminary report, which recommended the dual concept of the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan and the Net Income Stabilization Account. I should say that this task force committee reported on a regular basis to the federal and provincial ministers of agriculture. They brought forward their progress reports along with their recommendations. We considered those at that time and gave the recommendations our particular blessing and encouraged them to continue.
Government Orders
They worked on this and a second report was presented in August 1990. Again, the federal and provincial ministers examined the work and the recommendation. In November, when meeting in Winnipeg, we agreed to the principles of the two new programs and attempted at that time to set in place the motions and the mechanisms to implement these two programs.
I want to take this opportunity to express on behalf of not only the federal government, but I am sure provincial governments as well, and I am sure many farmers, to thank all of those who participated in this exercise. They gave of their time and their talents at considerable expense and inconvenience to themselves to come together in an attempt to devise a program that would not only serve the short-term and medium-term problems, but hopefully to provide a policy framework that would allow us to strengthen our industry and provide some predictability and some stability for the future.
It is important to remember that this committee was comprised of some 33 members. They were not bureaucrats working in isolation. They were not politicians working in isolation. The exercise was open. It was transparent. Of the 33 members of this committee, 19 of them were farmers, along with eight provincial and six federal government officials.
The committee studied eight different proposals before it came up with this recommendation. These proposals and various ideas and thoughts were advanced by industry organizations, by academics, by governments, so what we really have here is a bit of a compromise, because in that sort of an environment there is a fair amount of give and take. But I think what we have here is a consensus that reflects to a large extent a program which producers really want.
I think it is fair to say that we have here a program that was designed from the ground up by fanners. The provinces and the federal government worked with them in the development of this initiative, and I am very pleased about the way in which it has developed. The process, as I said, was transparent. All approaches and ideas were considered and again I say, as I have said on so many other occasions, I do believe that this reflects a unique approach to public policy-making in this country, and I think together we have designed a landmark

March 7, 1991
Government Orders
program which should minimize the need for ad hoc assistance.
If this program does work-and I think it will-I think we will clearly establish and demonstrate that in an era of co-operation we can bring diverse points of view together and we can come together as a very diverse nation to develop a policy that is national in scope but that at the same time, takes account of the regional strengths and the regional diversities of this great land.
We have tried to work toward the development of a national agrifood policy. It was started by my predecessor when the national agricultural strategy was first announced, and since that time we have tried to build upon the principles that were agreed to by the federal and provincial governments.
Since I have been Minister of Agriculture, I have had eight different formal meetings with my counterparts, the provincial ministers of agriculture. We have had many, many bilateral meetings with individual ministers and groups of ministers. When you couple that with the tremendous number of meetings that we have with farm organizations, commodity groups and individual farmers, it clearly has opened up the process. I think we have an environment and a mood out there, while we are facing some very serious difficulties. I do not think that we approached the problem with the idea that any one group, any one political party or any one political administration or government has all the right answers, has all the perfect solutions.
We are trying to labour together in looking at the problems and examining what we are doing and trying to determine what we can do better, in an attempt to provide a better future for Canadian agriculture.
The new safety net will deliver assistance equitably to farmers in all regions while at the same time encouraging good management practices based upon long-term market trends. The two components of this new safety net, as I have said before, the gross revenue insurance plan and the net income stabilization account will give farmers the kind of program they really need for the long term and the kind of program that they, the farmers, have been asking for.
It is quite obvious as we have gone through the last four or five years that the existing safety net and
stabilization programs that we have had in place were inadequate to deal with the very serious difficulties that we have faced in agriculture. Hence, we were required to come up from time to time with various ad hoc programs which had to be designed to meet a certain problem that occurred, a problem that was not covered by the existing legislation or programs that we have had in place.
Indeed, the federal government, under the leadership of our Prime Minister over the past few years has provided unprecedented assistance to our farmers. This kind of assistance was designed to meet a specific need. But whenever you design a program after the fact, there are always inequities. First of all, these kinds of programs are not easy to design, not easy to administer and not easy to distribute effectively and equitably.
We have had to do this and I think that all farmers, governments and literally everyone involved in agriculture, wanted us to look at ways and means of providing a more stable future, improved programs that would allow farmers to plan on the basis of their market intelligence, their managerial expertise, plus the known support that would be there under the government programs. The various programs we have had to come up with have covered an array of situations. For example, the Special Canadian Grains Program, the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program, the Special Income Assistance Program, the Cash Flow Enhancement Program, the Livestock Drought Program. We have had programs for grasshoppers. We have had programs for floods. We have had programs for the fruit industry.
We have gone through a period, and I know colleagues will share this with me, that in many respects, has been worse than the dirty thirties in terms of drought conditions and in terms of price.
Just today, we are working out an eradication and a compensation program for the potato industry, particularly, in the province of Prince Edward Island, which has been devastated by a virus that has affected that industry. We have learned very, very quickly in dealing with this process, if wheat is important to Saskatchewan, potatoes are as important to the province of Prince Edward Island. We recognize that and we are dealing with it, again in a co-operative fashion.

Yes, there has been some political grandstanding and some political finger pointing. The fact of the matter is that the job we must do is rid ourselves of the virus, eradicate it and get on with the job of restoring normal production and normal trading patterns, and that is precisely what we are doing.
In the budget of last week, an additional $1.3 billion of new money has been set aside for producers in difficulty. I think this demonstrates another clear example of this government's commitment to the agriculture industry and, particularly, to the farmers.
The long-term programs like the Western Grain Stabilization and Agricultural Stabilization Act, which have been in place for some time, while they have provided some stability and some support for our producers, obviously were unable to deal with the catastrophic and prolonged situation that our industry faced in the last half of the 1980s and the early 1990s.
The Western Grain Stabilization Act was established in 1976 to provide income stability for grain farmers in western Canada. The program was created to counteract the wide swings in cash receipts that are an all too important feature of the grains and oilseeds sector. The fluctuations in cash flow can have a serious effect, as we all know, on a prairie economy, and particularly on the grains and oilseeds sector. So, it is important to have these kinds of mechanisms in place.
What the Western Grain Stabilization Act provides to the grains and oilseeds sector, the Agricultural Stabilization Act does for producers of a wide variety of commodities outside those grains produced under the aegis of the Canadian Wheat Board. And while, as I said, these programs have provided valuable support to farmers across the country, they have been unable to cushion farmers against the low international prices and reduced yields of the 1980s.
What is more disturbing about it is that we are not precisely sure how long this condition will continue. So, it is important for us to look at this, not only in the immediate term, but in the long term.
As we know, the first indication of the problems we now face emerged in 1985 when the European Community and the United States began a struggle over their respective market shares of the world grain and oilseeds market. They fought their battle in the marketplace with the backing of their treasuries and Canada and other
Government Orders
mid-sized grain exporters watched as grain prices tumbled. We are the victims of the $245 billion a year subsidy war that is going on right now, as I speak.
The price of wheat dropped from $222 a tonne in 1980-81 to $120 a tonne in 1986-87. This downward price spiral was reflected in the Canadian Wheat Board initial prices for the 1986-87 crop year. It was clear that the excessive use of trade distorting export subsidies by the European Community and retaliation by the United States would translate into a major loss of income for our grains and oilseeds producer, a loss which went well beyond the scope of the WGSA and the ASA programs.
So, we were faced with responding to these concerns. We got together with farm groups to see what could be done. We analysed the scope of the problem and determined that producers would need a billion dollars in support from them for the effects of falling prices. In October 1986, the Prime Minister made a commitment to provide that kind of support.
This was duplicated through the special Canadian Grains Program wherein another $1.1 billion was committed in the following year.
In 1988, prices strengthened somewhat so there was no need for another special grains program. However, that spring in many parts of the country, including the prairies, parts of southern Ontario and Quebec, suffered a very severe drought which devastated yields.
Again, farmers faced financial difficulty and again the federal government stepped in. In November 1988, after a thorough examination of the extent of the losses, we announced the $850 million Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program.
The amounts of moneys that have been provided by the federal government in support of agriculture between the periods 1985 to 1989 total just under $22 billion, and almost $12 billion provided to the grains and oilseeds producers.
Now the need for help to the farm sector continues today. International grains and oilseeds prices are down and our Canadian producers are suffering. This again is largely because of the continuation of the trade war between the United States and the European Community.

Government Orders
I wish to give some idea of the magnitude, which I am sure most colleagues in this House who follow agriculture are very much aware of, but it is important to state it for the record. For example, the European Community wheat export rebates went from $44 a tonne in July 1989 to $116 in July 1990 and reached approximately $200 a tonne in January 1991. In the same period, United States export enhancement bonuses went from an average of just under $19 a tonne in 1989 to $28 a tonne in 1990, and we now have topped the $50 mark, $50 to $55 a tonne.
Last year the European Community spent $4.3 billion in export subsidies on cereals, and last month the U.S. administration asked Congress to increase its cap on the Export Enhancement Program from $425 million U.S. to $900 million. We now have wheat selling in the neighbourhood of $100 a tonne, although there was some encouraging news last week that wheat prices have strengthened somewhat and let us hope that that trend continues.
Last year this government implemented two new programs to help farmers cope with this situation. Last March we announced a $500 million special assistance program and this was in response to the problems stemming from the international situation, successive years of drought, lingering debt load and high input costs.
We also at that time indicated our intention to continue to continue and expand the Canadian Rural Transition Program which has provided assistance to some 3,500 farmers. We enhanced the Farm Debt Review Board process which has provided assistance to some 11,000 farmers and we brought in place an Equity Leasing Program which, heretofore, has assisted some 400 to 500 producers in re-establishing themselves on the farm.
In October of last year, after we witnessed the second largest crop in the history of Canada, some 60 million tonnes, we announced, with obviously a clogged system and deliveries not running up to par, a cash flow enhancement program to provide interest rate relief to farmers for their unsold crops. This program will provide some $1.5 billion of interest-free cash to the farm economy. It will cost the federal government somewhere in the order of $100 million.
In dealing with the problems and the response, and the uncertainty about what kind of program and when a program would be designed to meet a specific condition, farmers continue to ask for predictable safety-net programs, that would provide equity to producers in all regions of the country. They also ask for programs that would help them manage their farms on their own and they wanted us to deal with this issue on an individual whole-farm approach. In other words, they wanted a safety net program brought in that could be used as a management and financial tool.
I think that the programs that we are trying to legislate today will help meet these needs.
The Gross Revenue Insurance Program will provide farmers with revenue protection. It builds upon conventional crop insurance by offering farmers price support as well as yield protection. For the 1991-1992 crop year GRIP will deliver similar benefits across the country although there very well may be some differences in program design from province to province. We have allowed for that flexibility to gain some experience and to try to adapt as close as possible without undermining the integrity of the principles. We tried to ensure that there would be similarity yet sufficient flexibility to address the unique characteristics of the industry in each specific province.
In under-current market conditions we expect that GRIP will trigger a pay-out something in the order of $2.7 billion for the 1991-92 crop year.
Fanners will be able to buy this price protection through crop insurance. They will continue to be able to buy their yield protection through crop insurance and price protection through the revenue insurance program.
I might add that the crop insurance program is working very well because this House had the opportunity of improving the crop insurance legislation which was passed last year.
Nothing will really change in the manner of how farmers sign up. They will go in and still continue to buy their crop insurance as they have done in other years but they will have an added feature which will be the revenue protection component and by enrolling in both crop insurance and the new revenue insurance plan fanners will guarantee their income per acre for each crop seeded.

Crop insurance premiums will continue to be shared 50 per cent by producers and 25 per cent by each of the federal and provincial governments.
With respect to the revenue insurance program, farmers will pay one-third of the revenue insurance premium. The province will pay 25 per cent and the federal government will pay the remaining 41 and two-thirds per cent.
The advantage of GRIP is that the farmers will be able to calculate their guaranteed total returns early in the spring and this is a bankable commodity. They will be able to take it to their lenders and assist them in making their credit arrangements for this year. This indeed was borne out by the chairman of the Royal Bank, Allan Thylor, who said: "From a lender's standpoint, it's a very positive move-.When your clients have that sort of protection against a crop-a guaranteed price-you've got something much better to work with than the risk-taking that goes without that sort of protection".
There again even without this bill being passed we have sent out a very positive signal to the lenders on whom producers rely and I think that is a good signal.
In addition GRIP offers predictable equitable support across all commodities and regions, and it provides coverage for farm-fed grain-something that the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act have never done.
The program targets assistance to the individual and is therefore a more efficient way, we believe, of providing assistance, and support is based on long-term market trends which encourage sound management decisions.
If there is anything that we could say in reviewing some of the programs that we have tried to design as best we could I think we would find that under this program the assistance will be targeted more specifically to the areas of need.
It will be much more cost effective in providing the kind of support that the producing community will need.
We expect the Gross Revenue Insurance Plan to go into deficit for the first few years of operation but, as in any insurance program, there will be times both of surplus and deficit. But, one of the objectives of the task force was to design a program that was actuarially sound.

Provinces have been cognizant of that, we have been cognizant of that, and the producers have been cognizant of that.
When we are looking at this program over the long term we expect it to be actuarially sound. Obviously, over a five-year period that would not be the case, but we are in this for the long haul and will continue to add refinements and improvements as the experience gained from the program would dictate that we should do.
NISA, the Net Income Stabilization Account, would let farmers set aside money in individual accounts with matching contributions from the federal and provincial governments. Farmers can take money out of their individual accounts when their margins fall below the level of the previous five years or when taxable income falls below $10,000. For the 1990 tax year the program is likely to trigger withdrawals of about $225 million, again aimed at those farmers who need it most.
That may be an over optimistic figure because, as I said earlier, I am somewhat disappointed that more provinces have not come on board the NISA program. That is not to say they have rejected it. They are considering it very seriously and I think we will have a fairly comprehensive coverage of the NISA program for the next year.
These programs which we are implementing here today, the GRIP and NISA concept, while it is applied specifically today to the grains and oilseeds, can be expanded to other programs. In fact, there is keen interest in the horticultural sector. We are engaged at this very moment in discussing how to bring the horticultural sector into the GRIP and NISA program.
We recognize that there are some concerns about the program, about its design and how it will influence farmers' decisions. But, this program is not an insurance policy to ensure against bad management decisions. It is really designed to reflect a producer's individual performance and we think that is good. If a farmer grows crops that are not suited to his region or suited to his capabilities, his coverage through crop insurance will be reduced and his premiums will increase over time.
We certainly have our share of critics, some genuine, some armchair. Some say it is too rich. Some say the program is not rich enough. I note that the cattlemen say they are going to choke on GRIP. I find that strange

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to Bill C-98, the Farm Income Protection Act, which the minister has outlined before the House today.
This bill provides for the most massive farm support programs, GRIP and NISA, which have ever been proposed to Canadian farmers. Obviously the government has very skilfully managed this program, putting it before Canadian farmers in such a way that the legislation before the House today provides a framework for the federal government to make agreements with the provinces and with producers.
This legislation does not spell out what the premiums will be for producers who want to make a contribution and participate in the program. It does not say what the benefits will be. In some ways, that is the program that farmers have before them. They know the general outline, but they do not know specifically the premiums they will pay or the benefits they will receive, even though the program is well down the road toward contributions.
Clearly GRIP and NISA have a number of aspects about it which are very appealing. The pay-outs are made, for instance, on farm fed grains. There is no requirement to sell grain within a particular crop year to be eligible for a payment. The range of eligible crops compared to the western grain stabilization fund has been expanded and the pay-outs are predictable. The period over which the estimates are being made have been expanded from five years to fifteen years.
For many producers in western Canada there is a great deal of uncertainty because of the massive sales program which has been taking place this winter. Really, the sizzle is being sold but the actual details are not there. When this bill is being studied in the committee stage, technically we will not have the details of GRIP or NISA program before us even there because we are talking about just a framework legislation for signing agreements.
There is no provision in this legislation, for instance, for the GRIP and NISA agreements, which are being put together between the provincial governments that want to participate, to come before the House for members of Parliament to debate or amend them. It is kind of an executive federalism where a deal is put together between the Prime Minister or the Minister of Agriculture

In the budget estimates last week which the Minister of Finance brought down, he suggested there was going to be $1.3 billion. The prairie pools and farm groups have suggested that there should be a deficiency payment of at least $1 billion, perhaps even $1.3 billion.

Yet, when the budget announcement was made, it is not clear exactly what that $1.3 billion will be used for. It is suggested in the minister's press release that it may be used for the Canadian Wheat Board shortfall. That has been variously estimated at $750 million to $1 billion. If there is a provincial election in Saskatchewan, there can be a deficiency payment made there.
There is a concern that politics is almost as important here to the government as a long-term stable support program for Canadian agriculture. That is what concerns western agricultural producers and to some extent, in other areas of the country as well, that we are really
dealing so much with a sizzle here, that we have to be careful that we do not create a program that is not nearly as workable as it should be.
For instance, the minister has outlined the criticisms of the program by agricultural economists and other groups. But I think we would have felt better if he had gone into some detail as to what mechanisms there were in the program. We are not dealing with that program here, we are dealing with enabling legislation. But clearly, this enabling legislation provides for those agreements. Those are the kinds of questions that everybody wants to see answered.
There is a great concern as well, that this legislation essentially is an off-loading kind of legislation. We have seen that the government's support programs have dropped by $1.8 billion during the last three years. This bill seems to move from programs like the Special Grains Program, like the ASA, like the drought assistance, which essentially were totally funded by the federal government, or in the case of Western Grain Stabilization Fund, 60 per cent by the federal government, to off-load onto the provinces and the producers.
Many people in Saskatchewan wonder, for instance, whether a program that is going to cost the producers and the provincial government something like 60 or 65 per cent by those groups, whether payments of $400, $500 or $600 million a year in that province can be sustained, when programs in the past were substantially funded by the federal government. Many people make the argument that if the low prices are due to international grain wars, then the federal government has a responsibility to fund a great deal, just as they have in the past under the Special Grains Program or as the United States government does under its program. Whereas, under this GRIP and NISA program, there is essentially something like 60 per cent or 65 per cent being funded by the producers and the provincial governments.
That calls into question whether this will really be a national program. Under ASA and the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, between those two programs, there was a so-called national arrangement for support. It is not to say that those programs are adequate. Clearly, the Western Grain Stabilization Fund to fight a grain war, an international trade war, was simply not capable of doing that.

Mr. Speaker, we are here today to discuss Bill C-98, a bill which integrates a number of programs in the agricultural area that have been in existence for some time. It will integrate the Western Grain Stabilization Act, the Crop Insurance
Government Orders
Act, the Agricultural Stabilization Act under this new legislation.
This is a continuation of a trend we have seen in the last number of years on the parliamentary level where governments are introducing umbrella legislation that effectively asks Parliament to give them the power to do almost anything they like by executive fiat.
This legislation is no different. It follows that scheme. It allows the federal government to make deals with the provinces and with farmers, through the provinces, to come to agreements on Gross Revenue Insurance Program, a Net Income Stabilization Account, and revenue insurance programs.
In brief what is contemplated as near as we can understand is that a Gross Revenue Insurance Program will be put into place in most of the grain and oilseeds areas this spring.
This would provide certain guarantees based on a 15 year index moving average price for each of the 18 covered commodities, which would have the effect of covering wheat at something over $4 or $4.15-in that range-with the percentage of coverage varying slightly from province to province.
On the prairies, it is conceived that the program would be 70 per cent of the index moving average price for those 18 commodities times the average yield as shown in crop insurance in those three prairie provinces. When we get into other parts of the country, there are some other options open. It is possible to use a system of price setting other than the index moving average price, to do a production expenditures model which may prove useful to provinces like British Columbia or Quebec, which are already using a cost of production type model to provide their stabilization programs. They may find that option of interest.
The program also permits the Net Income Stabilization Account which still seems to be in a certain amount of flux. The idea there that seems to be public is that the farmers would pay half of this. The federal and provincial governments would split the other half of the cost.
Frankly, I am not up to date on what the Department of Finance has ruled. The origin of this was to make a self-insurance kind of program which would be attractive to those areas that do not suffer huge fluctuations in production.
