It is a little bit like the old poem that was in our readers when I was in school a long time ago of the seven blind men and the elephant. The seven blind men approached the elephant, and each one found a different part of the elephant to touch. They came to quite wrong conclusions as to what it was in front of them.
Some running into the belly thought it was a wall. Another feeling the tail thought it was like a rope. Another grasping a leg felt the elephant was like a tree. Another feeling its ear thought that the elephant was very like a fan, et cetera.
I suppose, to a certain extent, that is what has happened with the reaction from the various farm organization and the various analysts around the country.
We have a publication from United Grain Growers which does an analysis on GRIP, as it is understood in western Canada at the moment. It concludes that GRIP will produce more acres of crop with lower yields due to fewer inputs being bought, because there is an incentive under GRIP with the current levels of pay-out guarantees to tiy one's best to hit an average yield. Do not go overboard to try to get yields, because it will only reduce
the amount of income that you have. There is a real disincentive to try for higher yields according to their analysis.
They also point out that there is potential, if there are no changes in the current proposals, to make a mess out of the specialty crops, to use their words. What they have said in their report is: "Even a glut of lentils would not prevent farmers from growing more lentils the following year. The support levels in GRIP are fairly static, declining slightly over time". That is because of it being an index moving average over 15 years even though the price this year might drop considerably because a glut of lentils would not show up; it would only be one-fifteenth of the value of the price in the coming year. There are some concerns expressed by some of the groups who have done their analysis on it up to this point.
They point out also that farmers will react not to market forces any more but the new reality will be that they will react to new incentives created by GRIP and these reactions will be to alter acres and to change production decisions.
As well, we have a report from a group of agricultural economists in Manitoba and Saskatchewan: Kraft, Fur-tan, Rosaasen, Gray and Weisensel. They conclude that the way the program is written now, the way that the agreements that are in the works, federal-provincial, tend in their opinion to favour wheat because it is the safest crop with a fairly high price guarantee. They provide two proposals in their discussion paper which would have the effect of giving all crops equal or similar advantage by using their wheat acreage base as a form of coverage, so it would not matter. The pay-out would be based on an acreage, so to speak, and the farmer could grow whichever crop he thought he would get the maximum return from the market as a result.
Alternatively to that, they provide a rather complex basket per acre approach which would tie in all of the crops that are generally grown in a region and make that the base coverage model. As well, the group of agricultural economists have concerns about the possibility of very large pay-outs because the program does not seem to have any upper limits. They point out that it is very realistically within the realm of possibility that someone who seeds 5,000 acres could be taking home $.25 million of government funds having put in $16,000 to $32,000 in this particular year, or not more than $50,000 in this
March 7, 1991

particular year as his share of payments. There are some concerns about that.
We have a paper submitted by the National Farmers' Union concerned about the long-term shifts that this program may create to rural communities. They are pointing out that there is a very real off-loading of federal responsibilities and costs on to the provinces and on to farmers. This is particularly difficult for those provinces and regions of the country that are basically rural, particularly costly to the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island where the farm output is very high and the population that is non-farming is relatively low compared to the rest of the country.
They express some concern for the regional sustainability of these very important regions of our country, especially since metropolitan areas require the food that these rural areas produce but are being allowed under this program to opt out of paying so much for the program and leaving those costs up to the rural areas themselves to raise. That concern is echoed somewhat by the Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba, the hon. Glen Findlay who says:
If grain prices continue the way they are there could be very significant debt.
He is talking about debt to his province. He goes on to say:
I think Manitoba has taken a more responsible approach because we want to know the exact fiscal responsibility to our taxpayers.
So, Manitoba is bargaining very hard-headedly as to the sharing of the program as far as it applies to GRIP and particularly to NISA.
All of this discussion, of course, has raised the attention of the political columnists, and we have a number of those who have given opinions on GRIP and NISA. I have one here from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. Les McPherson is a columnist there and I hope he is talking tongue in cheek. He presents his solution to the farm problem thus: "Money could be collected in the cities, loaded into grain cars and hauled by railway to rural elevators. Then, whenever a farmer needed more money he would only have to drive his grain truck to the nearest elevator and load her up. Back on the farm he would simply use his auger to unload his money from his truck into a granary. The beauty of this approach is that it is self-limiting. When a farmer's granary is filled with
Government Orders
money he simply would not qualify for any more subsidies."
Now that may be a bit tongue in cheek, but it also does, unfortunately, reflect a growing opinion in those parts of Canada that are not farming and are not more directly dependent on farming, as to what the whole idea is behind transfers of tax dollars to cover expenditures that farmers have to make in order to produce food.
That goes beyond just Les McPherson. Dale Eisler of the Leader-Post, who is considered to be a serious political columnist, did an analysis on the Net Income Stabilization Account, NISA, in which he argued fairly strongly that NISA is a special consideration that nonfarmers should say no to.
So there is some growing concern from some of the press at least that these programs are very expensive and that taxpayers should not be concerned about continuing the very large pay-outs and large pay-outs are of concern.
I think it would be particularly difficult to explain and sustain the kind of pay-out that Furtan and Kraft look at in their proposal when they say that there should probably be a cap on this because there were caps on WGSA and on the ASA programs that this program supplants. It is hard to explain $250,000 of government funds going into one producer, even though I understand why that producer is probably going to need most of that money.
We have not had much discussion, though the minister did refer to it, as to what the third line of defence is going to be. Even in the country, we are only aware that there are a number of subcommittees working on the so-called third line of defence which was originally perceived to be an established program that would take care of disasters, whether they were international price disasters or weather disasters that were quite beyond the normal ability of these long-term programs, like GRIP and NISA, to look after.
What we are seeing is that the third line of defence is much broader than that. We have subcommittees looking into soil saving programs for regrassing and reforestation. We are not sure whether the third line of this defence also includes encouragement or assistance to have social shifts out of agriculture, but some comments

March 7, 1991
Government Orders
in the realm of third line of defence make it sound as if that might be part of the program. Some third line of defence programs are looking at development of alternative employment in rural areas to diversify into something either related to agriculture or completely unrelated, as long as it provides jobs.
Some of the third line discussions seem to be looking at assistance with diversification and breaking the grain dependence of some areas in Canada.
Over all, the bill before us is broad enough and vague enough that is is very difficult to be opposed to it. There is nothing there to oppose. There is very little there to support either. It is quite nebulous. It is quite wraith-like in its presentation. It will take form as federal-provincial agreements are signed and as those are made public. We presume that they will eventually be made public. Until that happens, it is almost anything one wants it to be. That is a problem we have with legislation. But, as I said at the outset, that is the new style of government of this particular government: to achieve from the Elouse of Commons the power to do anything it wants and then go on from there to run the country.
We are prepared to allow it to go quite quickly to the agriculture committee for review. In the committee we can seek answers, clarifications and perhaps discuss amendments and some of the merits of amendments that have already been proposed by some of the groups I quoted earlier in my remarks. We can perhaps get the Department of Finance in to explain what it has done to NISA and why it thinks it should not be a self-insurance program but instead a kind of farmers' RRSP or a special retirement fund or whatever it will be used for under what I understand are the current rulings with regard to it.
We will have to look at questions of choice. I was pleased to hear the minister say that no one has one perfect solution. That is particularly reassuring to my ears, because when I hear GRIP and NISA being discussed in my province of Saskatchewan I get the impression that the year after next we will have basically two choices. We can either participate in GRIP and NISA or we can opt out and, if we opt out, we will not be
eligible any more for any other kind of government assistance.
It is no longer clear that one can take either GRIP or NISA. Apparently one will not be able to continue with crop insurance and NISA, which is an option a lot of people in the more stable production areas find to be a useful and viable alternative.
I see the member from Assiniboia looking very puzzled. Perhaps he has not done all of the calculations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: You meant GRIP, not NISA.

Crop insurance and GRIP. The word we are getting so far is that crop insurance will exist under GRIP in two years and that it will not be possible to have a NISA plus crop insurance after two years. That restricts choice considerably, because once he does the economics of it he would find, as my preliminary discussions have discovered, that once outside the more drought ridden parts of the prairies there is not a lot to be gained from joining GRIP. Yet, we are not particularly keen to get out of crop insurance for the odd year when we have hail or frost.
Unfortunately, a lot of the decisions on these programs are being dominated by King Wheat in the southern prairies without reference to the rest of the country, and the rest of the country produces a lot of farm goods as well.
If there are going to be choices, I hope that in the committee we will be able to convince the government and the contracting parties that they should be recognizing that there are more farmers than just wheat farmers.
The questions of cost are also high on farmers' minds, as well as ministers of agriculture. I already quoted the hon. Glen Findlay from Manitoba, but I have been getting calls from farmers in the western part of the province saying that this could be a very costly program for them, that they have no choice but to be in or out. One woman said that this could cost her farm $60,000 to $80,000 in annual premiums and, perhaps better uses could be found for that money.
They want a clear understanding of what the cost is, what they might get out of it. They are quite cognizant that they might get nothing. This coming year, even though I expect, along with most grains analysts, a very low price for wheat, probably about $2.50 or perhaps
March 7, 1991

even lower, and given that GRIP covers $4.15 you would think that it would be a sure thing for a pay-out. But this is a gross revenue insurance program, so it is price times yield.
Even though the price may be one-half what the target price is, if the yield is double a normal crop, you would have produced yourself out of a pay-out. You may not be able to sell it, but that does not matter to this program. You would simply be sitting there with bins full of grain and no money, and probably complaining and yelling for the kind of solution that Les MacPherson in the Star Phoenix was offering: to shovel out money and send car loads to the rest of the bins. Now, because they are already full, there would not be room, I suppose.
Anyhow, those are some of the questions that are being asked. At committee I want to find out more about the assumptions that are being used to achieve what are described as actuarially sound premiums, because some of the premium prices I have been hearing sound as if the government is going to have great difficulty in keeping the fund out of deep debt for a long time.
I am concerned about that because this legislation appears to be intending to integrate the debt that is already there in the western grain stabilization fund account which, on February 1, was approximately $1.1 billion. I think the new act will also probably be required to absorb-though it is up to the cabinet to decide in both cases-the reinsurance fund debt which exists under crop insurance legislation. That is $471 million of debt as well. It is not expected to get itself out of trouble for at least six years, and under this program it may take quite a lot longer than that.
I want to know more about what sorts of arrangements are being made, whether the government is using a 15-year cycle, a 30-year cycle, or whether it is trying to keep program actuarially sound over 10 or 15 years.
There are going to be questions in committee about the cost. Also there will be the question of equity to smaller agriculturally dependent provinces, the shifting and offloading of the cost of food on to the areas that produce the food. Essentially what we are doing when we shift the cost of these programs, which have traditionally in this country been mainly federal in order to sustain prices and look after export problems because there are many metropolitan areas in this country that have a larger income and tax base, and need this food.
Government Orders
This program and this government are proposing-the program does not force them to; it is the kind of deals it is getting into-to make provinces like Saskatchewan carry a very high per capita debt each year in order to get GRIP; to make Manitoba carry a very high per capita debt each year in order to get GRIP and NISA. The same will apply to Prince Edward Island if the program is expanded to include potatoes.
These are questions that have to be dealt with.
Also, we have questions about GATT conformity. We were told by the minister-and I tend to concur-that the legislation itself is not breaking any GATT rules, but the agreements that have been talked about, I believe, are. I believe those are, as they say, "GATIhble". Some of our products will be subject to countervail and dumping actions as a result, particularly if we continue with the program as it is now where, as some analysts have pointed out, it has a wheat bias. If we do not take that wheat bias out, our wheat could very well be countervailed.
We have to know fairly soon, whether in committee or in this House. Somewhere the government is going to have to address the very real problem of the one-year GATT payments. Even if GRIP and NISA come into play, the programs will not be putting very much money into farmers' pockets until some time in 1992.
The last government payment to help us fight, sustain, and live through the American-European grain war occurred in July to September across the country, and there will be over a year's lapse in assistance. That gap has to be filled, and this government has to decide very quickly how that is going to be done and when it is going to be done.
Finally, there are questions of sustainability for rural communities, not just sustainable in the economic sense and not just sustainable in the environmental sense. But, if we are going to talk about sustainability in the environmental sense, let's remember that people are part of the environment too. The communities that those people are trying to sustain in those rural areas are also part of their environment; not only their ecological environment but their social environment. These programs that are being developed have to reflect that.

March 7, 1991
In conclusion, I am prepared to let this go fairly quickly to committee so that the vague assertions of this legislation can be clarified. Hopefully, the agreements that are arrived at between now and the end of the legislation will be made public, and then perhaps the committee will have a better idea of how this dream and this myth can become a reality. Until then, nobody can be particularly helpful with their criticism of this legislation. I hope we can find those answers in committee and that the government is willing to listen to proposed amendments, not only from our side of the House but also as proposed by farm groups, academics and individuals.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It being 1:17 p.m., I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
The House took recess at 1:17 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, while the western world, northern nations of the world, concerned themselves with the crisis and ensuing war in the Middle East, Third World nations, southern nations, have become more and more convinced that the world has passed them by. Already crippled by the financing burdens of their international debts, the gulf war has created calamitous conditions in dozens of Third World countries as a result of increased oil prices and the loss of wage earnings from their expatriate workers in the gulf region.
For the third year in a row, the Canadian government budget has cut Official Development Assistance to Third World countries. Here in Canada families in poverty, including one in six of Canada's children, waited in vain for a sign of concern. Instead of programs to lift our Canadian poor into productive, dignified, secure futures,
the already fragile social safety nets were further weakened by this government's last budget.
Neglect of the priority needs of both developing Canadian citizens, our children and youth, and developing nations is to threaten the well-being and security of Canada's future as surely as is the neglect of our national debt.
What we criticize today is not the government's focus upon the need to eliminate our debt, but the inappropriate and short-sighted priorities of the government in achieving its objectives. Two plus more wrongs do not make a right.

Mr. Speaker, the latest budget has revealed that while Canada's cultural sector is reeling from $18 million in cuts, the Department of Communications has awarded itself an increase of over $41 million, the lion's share of which goes into operating expenses.
Using $41 million for operating expenses while starving Canadian culture is tantamount to a slap in the face for all the dedicated and talented artists in Canada who continue to live well below the poverty line.
The minister should re-examine his priorities. When stalwarts of Canadian culture like the CBC are slashed $108 million and funding for Canada Council is frozen since 1986, how can the minister justify a 13 per cent increase to his department's bureaucracy?
The minister promised last fall to go to cabinet for more funds for Canada's cultural community, but what he neglected to explain was that he would use this money to pump up his own bureaucracy and lavish lifestyle, and not to the benefit of Canada's cultural community.

Mr. Speaker, it is my sincere wish that all members of Parliament will support the rapid passage of Bill C-98, the Farm
March 7, 1991

Income Protection Act. This legislation provides a basic framework under which GRIP and NISA will function.
In western Canada, 70 to 80 per cent of all agricultural receipts are from export trade, 75 to 85 per cent of Canadian wheat is exported, as is 60 to 70 per cent of Canadian canola.
As we all know, the international agricultural subsidy war is having a disastrous impact on the economy of Canadian agriculture. There is no question that the fate of Canada's most efficient and effective industry, that is Canadian agriculture, is beyond the control of the producers. A more stable agricultural sector provides for more viability in our cities, towns and communities. Hence this stability of utmost importance to our small business sector as well.
In Saskatchewan there are critics who claim this process is too complex and too time consuming. These same critics are short of alternatives, short of logical alternatives that must encompass Canada's entire agricultural sector and be responsible to all Canadian taxpayers.
Those critics and the media that pay heed to shallow criticisms do nothing to solve this problem that must be addressed by all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to read into the parliamentary record the following resolution of the town of Springhill, Nova Scotia.
Whereas the Town of Springhill citizenry, during past major conflicts, participated at the highest level of enrolment in the Armed Forces per capita in Canada-be it resolved the Tbwn of Springhill citizenry support the role the Government of Canada has taken in support of the United Nations war effort in the Persian Gulf, and be it further resolved the Tbwn of Springhill adopts the ships' companies of the HMCS Protecteur, the HMCS Alhabaskan and the HMCS Terra Nova as honorary citizens of the Town of Springhill.
All three ships' personnel, military and civilian, will be adopted by the town of Springhill and will receive a certificate to commemorate the occasion.
Springhill has certainly found a unique way to show the pride and appreciation of all Canadians for a job
extremely well done by our Armed Forces in the Persian Gulf.

Mr. Speaker, last year, 183,732 Soviet Jews were allowed to leave the Soviet Union to go to Israel. Over the next two years we expect that there will be one million Soviet Jews going to Israel.
The problem is one of absorption and housing in Israel itself. The war destroyed between 3,300 and 7,000 housing units in Israel.
The U.S. and European community are providing aid of over $1.3 billion to Israel. Canada is providing aid to Jordan, Egypt, and Iraq. We have to help the Soviet Jews.
There are disturbing trends in the Soviet Union: new examples of anti-Semitism, new examples of a hard line being taken. How long do we know the door will be open? We have to do the best we can, otherwise the plight of the Soviet Jews might be forever on the conscience of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow women throughout the world will stop to consider and celebrate the progress they have made on the road to equality.
International Woman's Day is unique in the history of women's struggle equality. It was celebrated for the first time in 1911, to commemorate a strike started by garment workers in New York to protest exploitation and intolerable working conditions.
In Canada, Quebec women have celebrated International Woman's Day since the early seventies. In 1978, women in the rest of Canada joined them, demonstrating their solidarity.
Mr. Speaker, this government wants to celebrate the efforts of women who are dedicated to the cause of equality in our society, and we remain firmly committed to promoting women's participation in the constitutional process and Canada's future.

March 7, 1991

Mr. Speaker, less than a year after his major constitutional initiative died, the Prime Minister has stated his intention to re-enter the constitutional fray because of the Allaire report, saying that he and his government speak for all Canadians in negotiations to formulate a new Canada, reConfederated, rebuilt, and reborn.
However, if this Prime Minister wishes to speak for all of Canada, then I urge him to seek a mandate on this issue for he has, unfortunately, no mandate and no credibility to lead any further constitutional negotiations. From Meech to Spicer, his road is one of failure.
Reformers would prefer Quebec to remain part of Canada. However, if the goals and aspirations of the people of Quebec are irreconcilable, then it is clear that Quebec and Canada must consider a mutually agreeable and more separate relationship.
The Reform Party of Canada will continue to communicate, to promote its view of a new Canada and to participate in any negotiations openly and honestly. Threats, bullying, and a failure to make a commitment to Canada beyond a mere economic commitment cannot long unite a country. They simply delay the inevitable.

Mr. Speaker, over the weekend the Minister of National Revenue stated before a public forum in Scarborough that he did not believe in multiculturalism. He added that he felt multiculturalism should eventually be phased out.

How can we believe a minister who says, in no uncertain terms, that he does not believe in multiculturalism? How can we assume he will know the standards set by this legislation and will apply them in his own department? How can we expect this government's commitment to be genuine, when there is dissension on this point in cabinet?

The Prime Minister must tell Canadians whose vision he shares: that of the Minister of National Revenue or that of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship.
As Canadians are trying to understand where this country is going, they need a clear message. The Minister of National Revenue must resign.

Mr. Speaker, too often industry gets a bad rap for being the polluters of our environment. It is time to take another look, because the world is changing and industry is proving that technology and the environment can operate in harmony.
Last month, Canon Canada, a business in Mississauga West, launched its clean earth campaign. Under this program, Canon will collect and recycle toner cartridges used in the company's laser beam printers and personal copiers. In Canada, it is estimated that 1.4 million cartridges will be eligible for recycling in 1991, which should help alleviate the land-fill problem.
This is a significant initiative, but Canon's commitment does not stop there. For every cartridge returned, the company will donate $1 to be shared by the World Wildlife Fund (Canada) and the Nature Conservancy of Canada.
My congratulations to the people at Canon for their vision and commitment to the environment, and for finding a new r word to go with reduce, reuse and recycle. Yes, remanufacturing may well be the way of the future.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister talks about restrictions on federal spending, but now, less than a year and a half before the next election, he has just authorized 30 Tory members to move to new offices.
March 7, 1991

One move may cost as much as $10,000, Mr. Speaker. This means it will cost the House of Commons nearly $300,000 to let 30 members play a new version of musical chairs.
How can the government justify this kind of frivolous spending in the face of budgetary cutbacks, when it has just asked its own employees and all Canadians to tighten their belts?
I urge the Prime Minister to set an example to Canadians and postpone these moves until after the next election.
An office does not the member make, and I think the Prime Minister, the President of the Treasury Board and the Conservative Party whip should put a stop to this foolishness immediately.

Mr. Speaker, it has been said that this government lacks a vision of Canada. As it enters into free trade negotiations and agreements with nations to our south, it has ignored our own future. It completely ignores Canada's north.
The budget, the government's estimates and its legislative program indicate a sad lack of knowledge and understanding of the vast potential within our borders.
Where is the northern vision of John Diefenbaker? Why have the goals and dreams of those who explored and settled our nation disappeared? Why is the idea of developing northern ports like Churchill simply ignored? Why have we not trained people to live and work profitably in the vast majority of Canada? Why have we looked at our geography and simply shrugged? Why has this lack of vision prevented Canada from including our native population in developing the north?
Is it any wonder why this nation struggles so much with finding its soul, when it has managed to ignore the very nature of our geographic heritage?

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is International Women's Day. Women in Canada have little cause to celebrate, particularly in Parliament.
Participation in the subcommittee looking at violence against women is ample evidence of the indifference of male MPs to this issue.
Indeed, many members of Parliament feel that the ability to blow apart rabbits rapidly is a higher priority than the need to reduce the carnage by guns from which women suffer disproportionately across this country.
Systemic sexual discrimination and harassment are rampant. Women are under-represented on key committees. Many parliamentary association executives, for example NATO, are private men's clubs. Signs and titles such as chairman identify this as a male place.
In a country where one in four women are sexually assaulted and 90 per cent of women experience sexual harassment in the work place, we as parliamentarians must act as a united force to combat this problem.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, friends in greed are friends indeed.
Claude Fontaine sits on the Board of Directors of Petro-Canada.
Claude Fontaine is a senior partner of Ogilvy Renault, barristers and solicitors.
Ogilvy Renault has been retained by the Government of Canada to assist in the privatization of, guess what, Petro-Canada.
Bernard Roy, appointed principal secretary to the Prime Minister in the past, now works for Ogilvy Renault. What another happy coincidence.
The Prime Minister, before becoming Prime Minister by way of Iron Ore, also practised law at Ogilvy Renault.
The Prime Minister and Bernard Roy were roommates at university.

March 7, 1991
Oral Questions
Friends will be friends. Greed will be greed. Tories are always the same.

Mr. Speaker, today over 200 students from across Canada representing the Jewish Students' Network and NAHON are in Ottawa for their annual lobby day.
The group led by Joey Felsen, Batia Tobin and Marla Silverberg are meeting with members of the House of Commons. Today, there is an urgent call for action due to the housing crisis already facing Israel and the large amount of damage caused by the Scud missile attacks.
The Government of Canada just recently confirmed its intention to extend humanitarian aid to Iraq. In a similar spirit the government should extend such aid to Israel, which has been an innocent victim throughout this war.
The Government of Canada has always supported the cause of Soviet Jewry and, as chairman of the Canadian Parliamentary Group for Soviet Jewry, along with all members of the House, we urge the Government of Canada to aid the people of Israel in rebuilding homes destroyed by the unprovoked attack by Iraq and, in addition, to build additional housing for the newly arrived Soviet Jews.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has published a booklet entitled Sustainable Development and the Northwest Atlantic Fishery.
The Law of the Sea is invoked to argue the case for restraint in catches. The Law of the Sea was designed to avoid crises in fisheries by affirming the responsibility of all nations to co-operate in conserving and managing fishery resources in the high seas.
The government hopes that the principles of the Law of the Sea will become "ingrained in the strategies of the world's fishing industries" so that ultimately "destructive overfishing will become as rare as it is unconscionable".
This is a great statement, but it is hollow because this government has not yet ratified the Law of the Sea. If the government wishes to be taken seriously on environmental issues, it should at last ratify the Law of the Sea and make sure that Canada does not become the laughing stock of the international community.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Yesterday the Prime Minister denied that there is a private committee of senior bureaucrats working on constitutional change behind closed doors.
Does he deny a front-page stoiy in The Globe and Mail of January 31, and I quote: "Teams of Deputy Ministers Work on new plan for Canada"?
Does he also deny the statement of his own minister of federal-provincial relations, Senator Lowell Murray, who said: "We're working in the federal government on our own constitutional program"?
Does he deny this statement of his own minister?
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend began by saying that I denied the existence of a private committee. I did no such thing. I denied the existence of a secret committee.
Oh, oh.
There is no secret committee. The best evidence of that is the newspaper quotes that my hon. friend has just cited It is not secret. It is public-
It is a private committee.
-and it is legitimate work being done by the Government of Canada to-
Bravo.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Unbelievable.
Only a Liberal would want deputy ministers not to work. We put them to work in the interests of Canada.

Hear, hear.
March 7, 1991

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the Prime Minister has learned nothing about the lessons from the death of Meech.

I wish the Prime Minister would explain what Senator Lowell Murray meant when he said that the government was working on a new plan for Canada. We are worried that once again, the Prime Minister may be working behind closed doors and setting us up for a new constitutional disaster.
Will the Prime Minister inform the House today what the exact terms of reference are of this committee? Will he identify the people on the committee? And finally, will he provide for public consultation on the Constitution? Public, not private and not secret.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons told us yesterday that the opposition parties have 9 full days, at their discretion, for debate on a subject they may select.
In the circumstances it would be quite normal, indeed appropriate and quite useful, if the Liberal party, with its present apparent concern for constitutional matters, were to initiate a debate on the Canadian Constitution and, perhaps for the first time, make known their perspective and positions regarding the reform or renewal of Canada. I think that would be a very constructive approach.
As far as the government is concerned, we have started a series of consultations across the country, through the Special Joint Beaudoin-Edwards Committee and the Spicer Commission. Committees at the provincial level are doing their job in this respect and, of course, a number of officials have been asked to consider these issues on behalf of the Canadian government. I think all this is quite normal. We have a responsibility, considering developments in other provinces, and I am thinking first of all of Quebec, to prepare a dossier or a series of dossiers that, in due time, will help parliamentarians make considered decisions to promote Canadian unity.

Mr. Speaker, the leader of the NDP falsely stated on national television last night that Parliament had voted on December 13 on a motion to expand the mandate of a parliamentary committee studying the amending formula. She also falsely stated that the Liberal Party had voted against it.
I am sure that the hon. leader of the NDP or her party at three o'clock will take the opportunity to correct the record. Unfortunately, no such vote ever took place either on December 13 or at any other time.
Therefore, my question to the Prime Minister is this. Given his reference in the previous question to the work of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, will he put a motion before the House of Commons today to expand the mandate of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee beyond the mere study of the amending formula? Will he put that motion today and show some leadership so that Parliament can have a public process, not a Prime Minister's process behind closed doors?

Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend knows, indeed as the country knows, I have a great deal of time for the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, but any lover's quarrels she has with the NDP should be resolved privately, not here on the floor of the House of Commons.
My friend says that the Beaudoin-Edwards committee is involved in mere study of the amending process. Nothing could be more important. It is inaccurate to suggest that this should be cast aside as mere study of the amending process.
My friend refers to the difficulties we had at Meech Lake; indeed we did. I was grateful then for her support and the support of her leader at the time, Mr. Turner, and grateful for the support of the NDP as well. On two occasions we managed to get the signatures of 10 provincial premiers on side to endorse the concepts contained in the Meech Lake Accord in 1987 and in 1990.
Will you expand the committee?

Subsequent to achieving those signatures, we had unanimity for the first time in constitutional history in Canada. We achieved unanimity, but we

March 7, 1991
Oral Questions
then had difficulty in respect of its ratification by a provincial legislature. I will acknowledge that. I also acknowledge that failure to ratify has brought about some very serious difficulties. But that was not the first failure that we have had constitutionally.
In 1982 the Constitution was repatriated without the endorsement of the province of Quebec and that too has brought about very serious difficulties which this government and this Parliament are trying to prevent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I want to observe that there has been on the part of the opposition some determination to keep the questions shorter and I hope that will be kept under consideration by all sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade. The government has not been open with the Canadian people about what it hopes to achieve in the trade negotiations involving Canada, the United States and Mexico. The minister says he seeks a single comprehensive agreement, not two or three agreements, but a single comprehensive agreement.
What will be in that single agreement? In the existing Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, energy is in. But both the Mexicans and the Americans have said that in a trilateral agreement, energy will be out. How can the government negotiate a single comprehensive agreement when Canada says that energy is in and Mexico says energy is out?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it must have taken a lot of energy to come up with that question.
Canada has not said energy is out or that anything is out in the proposed negotiations between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico. There will be no negotiation until and unless the U.S. Congress approves the fast-track authority that President Bush has asked them for. So it is not anticipated that negotiations could begin until the end of May or early June.
Mexico has not said that energy is out or whether energy is in. But we all know that Mexico has a very sensitive concern about the ownership of oil. They have said that discussions about the ownership of oil are out
because the Mexican Constitution is in. We have said that we are not going to negotiate the terms of the Mexican Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, the minister continues to obscure the discussions and the Canadian people are no wiser from his answer than they were five minutes ago about what it is they expect.
Yesterday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated that the remaining limits of foreign investment in the energy industry should be removed. The Minister for International Trade has said repeatedly that the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement does not need to be reopened. The Mexicans say that energy is not in. Canada now says that the remaining provisions in the energy section, Chapter 19 of the free trade agreement, should be reopened.
Will the Minister for International Trade state, once and for all, what it is that Canada seeks in these negotiations and will energy be on the table or not?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any proper subject for the negotiations on trade will be on the table to be discussed. Whether Canada, Mexico or the U.S. agrees to any particular side of an issue will have to be decided when the issue arises. We will agree to anything that is in the national interests of Canada, but we will not agree to anything that is not.
With respect to investment, I am glad to report that investment in Canada has increased greatly as a result of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and we would anticipate this would be even more so under a North American free trade agreement.
I am glad to see that my hon. colleague agrees with me, that foreign investment is good for Canada. It creates jobs and we have been able to get Canada going again as a result of our attitude towards foreign investment.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the Minister of Finance said that we needed the executive tax deduction, and I will quote the minister: "We have a tax system in Canada that we must maintain in a
March 7, 1991

competitive way with those of other countries, in particular, the United States."
Does the Prime Minister agree with this absurd excuse? Do we have to cut health care so that executives can have a free lunch while hospital waiting lists are getting longer and longer?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I also congratulate the hon. member. I believe that yesterday, the Minister of Finance was talking about tax shelters. I think that was one of the answers he gave to questions on that subject. In fact, the Canadian government has eliminated an impressive number of tax shelters which, in the past, tended to stew the equity of our tax system and the government has turned it into a much fairer national instrument, especially as far as the neediest in our society are concerned. That was the purpose of tax reform, and the minister mentioned a number of examples that are in fact quite the reverse of the point raised by the hon. member from Winnipeg.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister will check the record, he will see that what was raised yesterday was the business and entertainment tax deduction. The Minister of Finance justified it on the basis that we had to be in step with the Americans on this, as we have to be on so many other things. It appears that the only differences we can have in our tax system is that we are allowed to be more regressive than they are with things like the GST, but we are not allowed to be more progressive than they are.
So, I ask the Prime Minister, is this not the first fruits of the free trade agreement? On top of that, why do we see the obscenity made known today that 42 chief executive officers were given a 4.2 per cent increase the day before the government announced a 3 per cent cap on Public Service wages? Why is that? How does the Prime Minister justify that in light of the rhetoric of the government about everybody doing their fair share?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I think this, Mr. Speaker, is much ado about nothing. The information
Oral Questions
provided by the hon. member may be interesting, but it is wrong.
I would like to remind the hon. member that for the heads of Crown corporations for the calendar year 1990, we received some months ago from an independent commission a recommendation to give them increases in excess of 6 per cent. We looked at that, not for the coming year, but for the calendar year 1990, and we decided that they would get the same as deputy ministers for the past year, 4.2 per cent. For the next three years, I can assure the hon. member that all Crown corporation heads will get 3 per cent like everybody else.

Mr. Speaker, the 1,400 railroaders in my riding who just learned that they will be laid off for three months this summer because of a downturn in revenues at CNR will be very impressed with that answer, that the government has managed to finesse a 4.2 per cent increase for the head of CN while they have to go on the street.
I go back to the Prime Minister. I have asked this of the Minister of Finance and he refuses to answer, so I ask the Prime Minister. On behalf of the government, would he please tell us why the Business Council on National Issues and all the corporations they represent were not asked to contribute one single penny to deficit reduction? What is the answer to that question? Is it because they donate so much money to the Conservative Party or what?
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend knows that as a result of the closing of these tax loopholes-
What closing of loopholes? Not one.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure hon. members would want to hear the response of the right hon. Prime Minister.

As a result of the closing of tax loopholes, there are, as the minister has pointed out, thousands of corporations today paying income tax that had never paid corporate income tax in the past in Canada, or paid it on a lesser scale. For example, the chartered banks of Canada, the insurance companies and others who were able to take advantage of various fiscal breaks, no longer can do so. And, for the first time in

March 7, 1991
Oral Questions
many, many years, if not decades, they are paying their fair share of taxes.
My hon. friend is scandalized by some statistics that he raises. Someone showed me-and I will get it for my hon. friend-a statistic about a group of employees working for one of the Public Service unions, because unions have employees themselves. They went on strike some months ago for a month asking for a 5 per cent increase. The union management said it was too high, you must settle for 3 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
In answering questions from the member for Hamilton East, the Prime Minister today acknowledged the presence and operation of a senior committee of officials dealing with the question of renewed federalism.
I want to ask the Prime Minister whether he would fully answer the question put by the member for Hamilton East.
In secret.

Yes, in secret, operating behind closed doors, reporting to the Prime Minister.
Will the Prime Minister tell the House today when this committee is scheduled to report to the Prime Minister. Will the Prime Minister also tell the House whether the report of the committee, the recommendations of the committee, will be made public so that the public will truly have an opportunity to participate in the constitution making process this time around.

Mr. Speaker, we are now going through a new phase. It is one of decreasing expectations. When my hon. friend began with this question two days ago, the committee was secret, then it declined to private, and today it is senior. He refers today to a senior committee of deputies. There is one, indeed there are probably many committees of deputy ministers doing various things throughout the Government of Canada. I hope they are.
You mean you do not know? You better find out.
You can never be sure, Mary.
Oh, oh.

If my hon. friend is suggesting that a senior group of officials cannot meet and advise the government of their point of view, this would be a unique burden to be placing on officials of any government. Normally, officers of a government are allowed to come together, pursuant to instructions from a minister and to meet outside of the television cameras and provide advice to their ministers, which is then rejected or accepted. It is the ministerial responsibility to accept the criticism or reject it on the floor of the House of Commons. That is entirely appropriate.
I do not think my hon. friend should be scandalized by the fact that indeed there are many committees of senior deputies at work on various aspects of Canada's ongoing problems. It is entirely normal and prudent that we do that and that they function the way they traditionally have for 123 years and then give advice to the ministers, who accept criticism on the floor of the House.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are not scandalized at the prospect of the deputy ministers meeting or their working or that they are giving advice to the Prime Minister.
What they are scandalized by is the notion that even as the Prime Minister tells the people of Canada that this time they will be involved in the Spicer commision, they are part of the public process, in back rooms behind closed doors, in private, in secret, a commission meets and there is no provision to involve Canadians in that process. That is what they are scandalized by.
Will the Prime Minister give a straight commitment to the people of Canada today that this time they will be involved, that the recommendations of this committee, the government's plan held in its hip pocket, for a change will be shared with the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, let me begin by giving, of course, the assurance to my hon. friend that there will be ample opportunity for the public and members' involvement in the evolution, not only of the constitutional provisions on the procedural side, not only with the Spicer commission,
March 7, 1991

but in other ways where we will have an opportunity to consult.
My hon. friend, however, raises an interesting question, and that is the question of any aspect of secrecy. He is asking me whether I would be ready to throw open the doors of these public servants' meetings to the television cameras. My answer to that is yes, if the Liberal caucus will open its doors when they discuss the Constitution and let us all see what goes on.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. The Canada-Mexico free trade proposal will have a tremendous impact on the environment. In the Cana-da-US agreement the minister failed to stress the environment. He must not make the same mistake twice. Mr. Speaker, my question is this: Can the minister give the House the assurance that he will insist that Mexican industry observes the same environmental criteria that will be, or are supposed to be, applied to Canadian industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member fails to recognize that these are different negotiations with the United States. We had a U.S-Canada trade negotiation which resulted in the brilliant U.S.-Canada free trade agreement that has been so productive and so beneficial to Canada.
Oh, oh.
Why do you not read the Canada West Foundation report, the Royal Bank report? You people do not read.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure hon. members would want the hon. minister to complete his answer.

Mr. Speaker, at the same time, there was a negotiation on environmental matters, led by the
Oral Questions
Prime Minister, which resulted in the clean air agreement that has in a sense been entered into by our two countries.
We have an environmental protocol with Mexico at the present time. If I have the chance, I will research that and pass on additional details to the hon. gentleman.
If there is any need of a negotiation or a treaty on the environment between Canada and Mexico, then we will do it as a separate negotiation, and with the same kind of success the Prime Minister had with President Bush and the United States.

Mr. Speaker, the minister talks about reading. It is pretty clear that he has not read the green plan.
In the absence of the Minister of the Environment who occasionally thinks about it, let me ask my the question of the Prime Minister.
Quoting from the green plan, the federal government requires environmental impact assessments for all proposals coming before cabinet for decision. A statement of the environmental implications of new policies will be made public at the time that the cabinet initiative is announced.
The Mexican initiative has been announced. The issue is: Will the Prime Minister force his reasonably bumptious and antique colleague to come out of the back room? Did the government make the environmental impact assessments that are called for in the green plan? Will the Prime Minister table the implications now, as he is honour bound to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is correct in his view of what the law is, then we are indeed in very significant difficulty because we are negotiating with 102 countries in the GATT on trade matters, and we have not made an environmental assessment of those 102 countries.
I guess we are doomed by the hon. member to a great deal of additional criticism in that connection. It is a trade negotiation. If we need an environmental negotiation, we will enter into an environmental negotiation with far greater success than the hon. gentleman's predecessor's ever had.
Oral Questions PAY EQUITY

March 7, 1991

Mr. Speaker, during a nationally televised debate at the time of the last federal election, the Prime Minister made a commitment and said that he had already set aside money for pay equity for women in the Public Service.
After what we heard in the budget last week, I want to ask the Prime Minister: In spite of the warnings in the budget, does he intend to keep that commitment to the women in the Public Service? Will he fulfil that commitment to women of Canada? Yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, without any hesitation, I can repeat the commitment of the government to pay equity.
As you know, we did something that former governments did not do. We settled for a very generous, honest and fair package. It is being contested. We will see where we are, but this is more than the Liberals did over I do not know how many years or decades of government.
We have committed ourselves to this. We have set aside in the budget the money necessary to continue that, and I can vouch that we will continue to proceed in this direction. It is the only good one in any case.

Mr. Speaker, today we learned that friends of the government, appointees of the government, get raises of tens of thousands of dollars while women, who are at the bottom of the economic system in this country, are told in the federal service that they get 3 per cent or they lose thousands of jobs.
And they lose thousands of jobs.

Can the Prime Minister assure this House that he will not compound this injustice to women in the federal civil service? Will he assure us that the job losses will not be women's jobs at the bottom of the economic order? Will he assure us that women will get pay equity and be fairly treated by this government, finally?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
I can only repeat that this government has not only spoken about these things but has acted. I would like to repeat that one of the
central issues that we have to be concerned with is that we cannot afford not to allow women to bring their full share not only to the federal civil service but to the whole society. I can assure the hon. member that the performance of the managers will be judged on their capacity to deal with these very important issues. We are committed to pay equity and it will be seen that we are, over the months.

Words are wonderful. Nearly seven years ago this Prime Minister, on national television, committed his government to economic equality for Canadian women. Today, those women still make 67 cents for every dollar made by men.
I want to know from this Prime Minister what became of this commitment. Is the Prime Minister satisfied with these statistics, and when will he keep his promise and act to seriously improve the economic status of Canadian women?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always feel badly when all a member can say is negative about the status of women in Canada as opposed to talking about the positive things. I am sure my hon. colleague is aware that there are today 900,000 more women working in this country and that there has been a 77 per cent increase in jobs in administration, management and professional jobs. In fact, there has been more than double the number of women working in those jobs. Fifty per cent of the students now in our colleges and universities are women.
Through the financial initiatives of this government- there are economic initiatives-indeed, the status of women is improving, and we should be encouraging our young women of this country to take advantage of the opportunities which exist for them out in the workplace.

Those advantages, Mr. Speaker, may exist somewhere, but one of the places they do not exist is the Public Service of Canada, unless either the minister or her Prime Minister is unfamiliar with the report of the public service, "Beneath The Veneer". In that report we are told that women who work in this Public Service are daily and constant victims
March 7, 1991

of systemic discrimination. There is no glass ceiling for men.
When is the Prime Minister-and I apologize for being negative-going to act meaningfully to end discrimination for women in his Public Service here in this country and fulfil his commitment?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for a very important question. I know that, as someone very committed to the cause of the promotion of women, she will be very interested to know that the day I was sworn in as Prime Minister, there were three women Deputy Ministers in Canada; there are today 21. There were two women serving as ambassadors; there are now 16. There were 37 women in the federal judiciary; there are now 79. The number of women serving on agencies, boards and commissions-the highest Order in Council appointments of the Government of Canada-has, in the space of six years, after 16 years of Liberal government, been increased by 107 per cent.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, in the Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade talks, Canadian culture will again be under attack.
American negotiator, Carla Hills, assured U.S. congressmen that they will get Canadian cultural industries this time, that giving a cultural exemption to Canada in the last round was a big mistake.
Will the Minister of International Trade assure Canadians that in any future trade talks that protection for Canadian cultural industries will be strengthened, and will not be weakened as suggested by the U.S. negotiator, Carla Hills?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the members of the House already know from the provisions of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement that this government is well capable of preserving the strength of Canadian culture and Canadian cultural agencies.
Mrs. Hills is simply expressing on behalf of the U.S. government its chagrin at having failed in the U.S.-Can-
Oral Questions
ada free trade negotiations in having got anywhere with reference to the Canadian cultural industry.
I can assure the hon. member that the Mexicans have exhibited no desire to make an assault upon Canadian culture, and as long as I am the trade minister she can depend upon it. Canadian culture is safe.

I know that beer is safer than Canadian culture and I know that we got strangled with clause 2005, so do not tell me what the condition of Canadian culture is, based on what the minister has to say. With the so-called cultural protections that this government has given us, and the minister knows this, our creators, our film makers, our magazines and newspapers and our book publishers are all at risk.
So my question to the Prime Minister, seeing as how he will not let his minister of culture do it-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member would put her question.

Mr. Speaker, I would kindly ask the Prime Minister to give serious consideration to reinstating a proper film distribution policy, to reinstate the postal subsidies for our magazines and our books, and to enforce Canadian control of the minister's famous Baie Comeau policy. Or, I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if he needs Carla Hills' permission.

Mr. Speaker, I can give the hon. member the assurance that the government's responsibility for cultural industries in general and this one in particular is being taken very seriously, that policies have been initiated, and that compared with the situation under the previous Liberal government, Canada's cultural industries are now in far better shape.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Justice.
Will the minister confirm that a consortium of companies, including General Motors of Canada and Diema-co, has recently signed a contract to export light armoured vehicles. The House saw those types of vehicles in the Oka crisis. They have machine guns on top

March 7, 1991
Oral Questions
of them. The contract is with Saudi Arabia and it is worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
We should confirm that the contract appears to stand in violation of Canadian law.
Is the government considering an amendment to the Criminal Code of Canada and the Export and Import Act to allow this deal to go through?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I told the House on December 20 in answer to a question from the hon. member for Kitchener in whose district the firm of Diemaco is located, the government is considering such an amendment. Diemaco is the manufacturer of automatic weapons and as a result of a technical problem in the Criminal Code, its business is interfered with. It has about 500 employees, I believe, in Kitchener and if that firm is to continue operating and supplying automatic weapons to the Canadian Armed Forces, it has to be able to enter into contracts with others outside Canada who pass the intense scrutiny and control that is given to this matter by the Department of External Affairs.
So, yes, that is under consideration as it has been for some time, as I explained in the House on December 20.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplemental question for the Prime Minister on this matter. His Secretary of State for External Affairs said the other day: "If there is one priority, one lesson which the world must learn from this war, it is that an unrestricted arms trade in this region, the Middle East, is no longer acceptable and constitutes a threat to the security of all members of the UN". I could also quote his letter to Perez de Cuellar on the matter of arms sales.
Instead, I want to ask the Prime Minister: Is this the time for Canada to be making a record arms sale to the Middle East and indeed, changing our existing gun control and export laws to do it?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are arms and then there are arms. We are discussing automatic weapons, that is rifles and other small arms of that nature, machine guns and the like which are necessary for armies, police forces and civil authorities to have if they are to be in a position to
keep order in their own countries. We are not discussing other offensive or horrendous weapons of war.
If hon. members will look at the report I tabled yesterday on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, they will see the small amount of arms exports that Canada does have and the careful system of controls there is. I can assure hon. members that the Secretary of State for External Affairs keeps a very close personal eye on this.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In light of the statement made last evening by President Bush putting forward a Middle East program, where he underlined the necessity of having a resolution of the Arab-Israeli dispute, I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he agrees with the statement that was made yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in Jordan, where he said that the PLO must have an important role in any Arab-Israeli peace negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, we were very pleased with the statement last night by President Bush because it in many ways supported very actively the positions that this government set out in a letter to Perez de Cuellar and then again on March 4 in regard to the position of the Government of Canada.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs yesterday, when you read the full remarks, was actually quite careful in respect of this sensitive matter, where he said there obviously has to be a representation by Palestinians and it will be Palestinians themselves who are best placed to determine who their representative should be. Then he went on to say that "In respect of the PLO, its authority I think there has been diminished by this war". I personally believe that the authority of the-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I hope hon. members will remember that yesterday a matter of order was raised as to the difficulty in many members not being able to get to the floor through Question Period. We are in the last few minutes, the Prime Minister is replying and I know that hon. members would want him to continue and conclude his
March 7, 1991

answer as soon as possible, so that perhaps I can recognize another member.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Obviously any durable resolution of this matter will require discussion between Israel and the Palestinians on the one hand, and Israel and its Arab neighbours on the other. The Palestinian people, as I have indicated in the past, will choose their leaders and their organizations in regard to any participation.
But I must say on behalf of the government that anyone who has looked at the position of the current leadership of the PLO, particularly in its support of Saddam Hussein and its cheering of Scud missiles as they rained on Israel, would have to conclude that the PLO and its leader, Mr. Arafat, have been substantially if not completely discredited as a result of their own actions.
Our strong dissatisfaction with the PLO position and statements on the gulf crisis has been stressed over recent months during official contacts in this regard. We acknowledge that there is an important role for the Palestinians to choose their own leadership, but our enthusiasm for the present PLO leadership is zero.

Mr. Speaker, whether the Prime Minister or the government is enthusiastic is not my question.
I was asking: Does he agree with the sentiments expressed yesterday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the PLO must have a role in helping to negotiate that?
It is a very important issue that is raised at this very sensitive time in trying to develop a peace resolution in the Middle East.
Mr. Speaker, I have just given the answer on behalf of the Government of Canada-
No, you haven't.
It is an important issue.
Explain that to Joe.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The right hon. Prime Minister.

If my hon. friend cares to examine it, he will see that there is nothing at all inconsistent in the
Privilege
principles that I have set out with the full context of the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
This has been the position of the Government of Canada and it remains the position of the Government of Canada.
All parliamentarians, those who supported the deployment of Canadian troops to the gulf and those who opposed, will agree that the conduct of the organization purporting to represent the Palestinians has by its very own actions, in my judgment, discredited itself over the course of these very difficult last number of weeks.
I am telling my hon. friend that this is the position of the Government of Canada. We are looking for peace, a durable peace. That peace must respect the security of Israel and it must also accommodate the legitimate rights of Palestinians. This is the way a peaceful solution can be brought about and Canada is committed to that process.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gave you notice earlier today with regard to a question of privilege concerning the comments made by the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party, which we believe has misrepresented the proceedings of this House with regard to the debate on Motion No. 25, on television last night.
From time to time mistakes in point of fact can be made but the-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond is rising on a question of privilege which involves the leader of the New Democratic Party.
As he well knows as an experienced parliamentarian and as other members know, in a matter of this sort we usually try to make some effort to have both of the parties in the Chamber.
I wonder if the hon. member for Kamloops could give me some indication as to whether it would be appropriate to continue at this time, or whether he would ask that we arrange an appropriate time for this matter to be raised when the hon. leader of the New Democratic

March 7, 1991
Business of the House
Party can be here. I will hear the hon. member for Kamloops on that point.

subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I might say I was a little disappointed in my hon. friend, the Liberal House leader, for not having the courtesy of informing us that this-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: I know that the hon. member for Kamloops will forgive me for saying that I did not want to start a debate. This is a request from the Speaker to the New Democratic Party, and I would like to know what its view is at the moment.

subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our view is simply that we ought to proceed as we always do on these kinds of issues and that they are raised and debated when the members involved are in the House.
I would like to say that the leader of the New Democratic Party will be in the House on Monday, and perhaps we can revisit this issue at that point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will abide by your advice and your ruling. The point is clear with regard to a misrepresentation of fact. I am sure, if I were given the opportunity, that the House leader for the New Democratic Party would want to avail himself of the opportunity to make a simple apology.

subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a simple apology? First, all I can say is that we have a long-standing tradition that if you are going to raise an issue about a member, you wait until he or she is in the House. On top of that, you would have the courtesy of informing the person with whom you are going to discuss some aspect, ahead of time.
We always do that. It is a tradition of this House. I am a little disappointed in my hon. friend that he did not make that effort.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF LEADER OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
I should point out that the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond has indicated his complete co-operation with the tradition which we have followed.
I take it, then, that we will hear this matter at the earliest convenience on Monday, and we will hear the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond further on that matter on Monday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be our intention today to complete second reading of the agricultural bill which is before the House. Should that not be completed by this evening, it would be our hope that it would be completed tomorrow, as well as Bill C-91 for tomorrow.
At this moment we would be looking at an Opposition Day on Monday. We are having ongoing discussions with the House leadership of the other parties. We will continue those discussions, and I think through that information we will be able to inform all members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I will also direct my remarks to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House. As he knows, last week in the House I asked the government when it would be introducing legislation on the northern tax benefit.
I have subsequently checked with our House leader, and it is not in the government's legislative program for the next couple of weeks to introduce that legislation.
I have also been informed that the Senate is going on a break. I would like to know what the government's plans are, in that a number of Canadians in communities across northern Canada want to fill in their income tax. They do not have the legislation passed by this House. Even if they fill in their income tax, there is no way the government is going to pay back any rebates owing to them.

We have been sitting here for a couple of weeks now. The Minister of Finance gave the press the wording of the legislation prior to the House coming back. Why has that legislation not been introduced in the House? Why has it not been put through the House by this time? Why has it not been done prior to the Senate taking another holiday?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons

On the same point and just to reassure the parliamentary secretary, we made that obvious to the Minister of Finance weeks ago and we made it obvious in the House last week. I would suggest that it is the government that is stalling on its own legislation.
